Eggs of the Indian roller are deposited within unlined cavities and incubated over a period of 17 to 19 days; under controlled incubation at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the precise age at hatching was recorded at 18 days [ab = 18 days], a duration that aligns closely with reports for other Coracias species occupying similar subtropical environments. The altricial hatchlings emerge at a relatively low mass; back-extrapolation from growth trajectories suggests a wet weight at birth of 14.7 grams [Wwb = 14.7 grams], which is modest compared to the ultimate size attained by adults during the post-juvenile phase. As the nestling progresses toward independence, the time since birth at fledging occurs at 32.5 days [tx = 32.5 days] when reared under typical ambient conditions maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], with the feather-growing nestling achieving sustained flight shortly thereafter.

Reaching sexual maturity marks a significant transition in the life history of the Indian roller. At the warm temperature regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty was determined to be 97.5 days [tp = 97.5 days], a developmental pace that permits birds hatched early in the breeding season to commence gonadal maturation before the onset of their first winter. While earlier reports suggesting a shorter interval of 30 to 35 days were based on observations of captive individuals under highly favorable nutritional regimes, the more extended estimate of 97.5 days likely reflects natural constraints on resource acquisition in the wild. Following the achievement of reproductive maturity, the sub-adult bird enters a period of non-breeding dispersal before initiating its own reproductive effort.

First breeding in the Indian roller is typically deferred until well after the individual reaches sexual maturity. Under the sustained thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at first brood was recorded at 730 days [tR = 730 days], indicating that most birds spend their entire first year and a significant portion of their second year as non-breeding floaters. This extended interval to first reproduction is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes extensive foraging experience and territory acquisition before investing in offspring. During this lengthy pre-breeding phase, the young adult continues to refine its hunting skills and strengthen its pair bond, laying the foundation for successful subsequent nesting attempts.

Once breeding commences, the Indian roller exhibits a moderate annual reproductive output. Under the ambient temperature regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], females typically produce 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch], and field surveys indicate that they complete approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year], reflecting the relatively short monsoon-spring breeding window available in the species' range. The total maximum reproduction rate derived from these parameters yields a modest yearly productivity. This clutch size is typical for tropical coraciiforms and is balanced against the substantial parental investment required to provision the developing altricial nestlings until they reach independence.

The eventual adult body size achieved by the Indian roller also influences its other life-history parameters. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches approximately 157.46 grams [Wwi = approximately 157.46 grams], a value consistent with published ranges from museum specimens that cite an adult mass of 166 to 167 grams. This relatively robust body mass is accompanied by a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 8.9 years [am = approximately 8.9 years] when maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a longevity that positions the Indian roller among the longer-lived members of its genus. The interplay between a deferred first reproduction, modest annual fecundity, and a multi-year lifespan suggests a life-history strategy adapted to environments where adult survival is relatively high and juvenile mortality is unpredictable.
